1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 35:12.
The words **Migdol**, **Tahpanhes**, and **Memphis** are the names of cities in Egypt, and the word **Pathros** is the name of a region in southern Egypt.

2.q: כֹּה אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל
2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 29:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:15.
See how you translated the similar expression in 26:2.

Yahweh says **there is no dweller in them** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that very few people still live in these cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and almost no one lives in them anymore]

3.note: Yahweh is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of their evil]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **anger**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to make me angry]

Yahweh is speaking as if the earlier generations of Israelites were the immediate **fathers** of the people he is addressing. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nor your forefathers]

4.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 29:19.
See how you translated **rising early and sending** in 25:4.

4.q: אַל נָ֣א תַעֲשׂ֗וּ אֵ֛ת דְּבַֽר הַ⁠תֹּעֵבָ֥ה הַ⁠זֹּ֖את אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׂנֵֽאתִי
4.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that you must not do this thing of abomination that I hate]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **thing** that is characterized by **abomination**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [this abominable thing]

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:24.
See how you translated this expression in 7:24.

Yahweh is speaking as if the people had been walking toward **their evil** and needed to **turn back** from it. He means that they needed to stop doing evil things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to stop doing their evil deeds]

6.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 42:18. Alternate translation: [And I was very angry, and I severely punished the people in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his anger as if it were a fire that **burned** in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. It means that his anger caused destruction and punishment there, as a fire destroys what it consumes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it destroyed]

The terms **a ruin** and **a desolation** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [completely ruined]

7.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:14.

7.q: לָ⁠מָה֩ אַתֶּ֨ם עֹשִׂ֜ים רָעָ֤ה גְדוֹלָה֙ אֶל נַפְשֹׁ֣תֵ⁠כֶ֔ם
7.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people for what they are doing. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. This rhetorical questions continues until the end of the next verse. Alternate translation: [You should not be doing great evil against your souls]

Yahweh is using **your souls** to represent the people themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against yourselves]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people would **cut off** other people the way someone cuts a branch off a tree. It means that they are causing these people to be destroyed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to cause to be destroyed from among yourselves]

Yahweh is referring to all of the people by naming two major components, **man and woman** and **child and nursing one**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everyone of every age]

8.note: If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **anger**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by making me angry]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:16.

It might seem that the expression **where you are going to sojourn there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [where you are going to sojourn]

8.q: לְמַ֨עַן֙ הַכְרִ֣ית לָ⁠כֶ֔ם וּ⁠לְמַ֤עַן הֱיֽוֹתְ⁠כֶם֙ לִ⁠קְלָלָ֣ה וּ⁠לְ⁠חֶרְפָּ֔ה
8.note: The phrase translated as **in order to** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [with the result that you cut off for yourselves, and with the result that you become a curse and a reproach]
See how you translated“ to cut yourselves off” in the previous verse.

Here, **a curse** represents the people of Judah as an example that others will mention when they curse someone, and **a reproach** represents them as people whom others will insult. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [an example that people use when they curse others and a people whom others insult]
See how you translated the similar expression in 26:6.

9.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the people for forgetting the evil things that they and their ancestors did. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You seem to have forgotten]
The pronoun **his** refers to each of **the kings of Judah**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the evils of the wives of each of those kings]

10.q: לֹ֣א דֻכְּא֔וּ עַ֖ד הַ⁠יּ֣וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֣א יָרְא֗וּ
10.note: Even though Yahweh is addressing the people of Judah directly, he is speaking of them in the third person as **They**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [You have not been crushed to this day, and you have not feared]

Yahweh is speaking as if the people should have been **crushed** like something that is broken into pieces. It means that they have not humbled themselves. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have not become humble to this day]

The expression **They have not been crushed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They have not humbled themselves]

Yahweh is speaking as if his **law** and his **statutes** were a path in which people could have **walked**. It means that the people have not lived in the way that his law and statutes require. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they have not lived according to my law and my statutes]

Here, **to the face of** represents “before,” meaning in the presence of the people. Yahweh means that he gave his law and statutes directly to them and to their ancestors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before you and before your fathers]

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 18:13.

**Behold me** is an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to set my face against you]

Yahweh is using **setting my face against you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “being determined to oppose you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [determined to oppose you and bring disaster] or [I am determined to oppose you and bring disaster]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **disaster**, you could express the same idea in another way as in the UST.

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if Yahweh would use a blade to **cut off** all Judah, like cutting a branch from a tree. It means that Yahweh will destroy all the people of Judah. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to wipe out] or [and to put an end to]

12.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 42:15.
See how you translated the similar expression in 42:22.

Here, **the sword** represents “war.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They will fall in battle … By war] or [They will be killed by enemy soldiers … By enemy soldiers]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:10.
See how you translated this expression in 42:18.

13.note: Yahweh is using **visit upon** as a common expression of the culture to mean “punish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:12.

14.note: The terms **a fugitive** and **a survivor** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [even a single person who escapes]

14.q: הֵ֜מָּה מְנַשְּׂאִ֤ים אֶת נַפְשָׁ⁠ם֙ לָ⁠שׁוּב֙ לָ⁠שֶׁ֣בֶת שָׁ֔ם
14.note: Yahweh is using **they are lifting up their soul** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they are longing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are yearning to return to dwell there]

14.q: כִּ֥י לֹֽא יָשׁ֖וּבוּ כִּ֥י אִם פְּלֵטִֽים
14.note: If it would appear in your language that Yahweh was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [For only fugitives will return]
See how you translated the similar expression in 22:27.
See how you translated the similar expression in 42:22.

15.note: Jeremiah is speaking of himself in the third person as **Jeremiah**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, Jeremiah]

16.q: הַ⁠דָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר דִּבַּ֥רְתָּ אֵלֵ֖י⁠נוּ בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה אֵינֶ֥⁠נּוּ שֹׁמְעִ֖ים אֵלֶֽי⁠ךָ
16.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **we are not listening to you** before the information about **The word that you have spoken to us in the name of Yahweh**. Alternate translation: [We are not listening to you about the word that you have spoken to us in the name of Yahweh]

Here, **in the name of Yahweh** represents “with the authority of Yahweh.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with the authority of Yahweh]
Here, **The word** represents what Yahweh has said by using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

17.note: The people are repeating forms of the verb **do** in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [For we will surely do]

17.q: אֶֽת כָּל הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר אֲשֶׁר יָצָ֣א מִ⁠פִּ֗י⁠נוּ
17.note: The people are using **every word that has gone out from our mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “everything that we have vowed to do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything that we have vowed to do]
See how you translated this name in 7:18.
Jeremiah’s hearers are using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST.
Here, **bread** represents “food” in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [food]

The people are using **we had good** as a common expression of the culture to mean “we prospered.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we did well]

The people are using **disaster we did not see** as a common expression of the culture to mean “we did not experience disaster.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and nothing bad happened to us]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **disaster**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and we did not experience anything bad happen]

18.note: See how you translated this name in 7:18.

The people say **we have lacked everything** and **by the sword and by the famine we have come to an end** as extreme statements for emphasis. They still had some things, and not all of them had died. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [we have lacked many things, and many of us have died by the sword and by the famine]
See how you translated the similar clause in 5:12.

19.note: Jeremiah is now introducing the women as the speakers of what follows, as the words **our husbands** show. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And when we women]

19.q: הֲ⁠מִֽ⁠בַּלְעֲדֵ֣י אֲנָשֵׁ֗י⁠נוּ עָשִׂ֨ינוּ לָ֤⁠הּ כַּוָּנִים֙ לְ⁠הַ֣עֲצִבָ֔⁠ה וְ⁠הַסֵּ֥ךְ לָ֖⁠הּ נְסָכִֽים
19.note: The women are using the question form to emphasize that their husbands knew about and approved of what they were doing. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [it was certainly with our husbands’ approval that we made for her cakes to copy her and pour out to her drink offerings!]

The **cakes** that the women made for the queen of the heavens were a kind of bread made in the shape of the goddess or marked with her image. If your readers would not be familiar with what these cakes were, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [loaves of bread shaped like her]
See how you translated this name in 7:18.

20.note: Here, **word** represents “what they said” to Jeremiah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [answering him with what they said]

21.q: הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא & אֹתָ⁠ם֙ זָכַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה וַֽ⁠תַּעֲלֶ֖ה עַל לִבּֽ⁠וֹ
21.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to emphasize that Yahweh did remember the incense that the people burned and that he thought about it. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has surely remembered them, and it has come to his heart!]

Jeremiah is using **it come to his heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he thought about it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and thought about them]

22.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 4:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 25:11.

23.note: Here, **the voice of Yahweh** represents “what Yahweh said.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to what Yahweh said]

Jeremiah is speaking of **this disaster** as if it were a living thing that could meet people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have experienced this disaster]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:6.

24.note: In this verse, the word **Judah** is singular in form, but it refers to all the people of Judah as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a plural expression such as “people of Judah.” Alternate translation: [all you Judeans]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4.

25.q: עָשֹׂ֨ה נַעֲשֶׂ֜ה אֶת נְדָרֵ֗י⁠נוּ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָדַ֨רְנוּ֙
25.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that you would certainly carry out the vows that you had vowed]

25.q: הָקֵ֤ים תָּקִ֨ימְנָה֙ אֶת נִדְרֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠עָשֹׂ֥ה תַעֲשֶׂ֖ינָה אֶת נִדְרֵי⁠כֶֽם
25.note: Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He is not encouraging the people to keep their vows, but he is warning them that he will punish them for doing so. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If you keep your vows and do what you vowed, I will certainly punish you]
The word **You** is masculine plural here because Yahweh is addressing the men of Judah, so use the masculine plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **your mouth** represents “your words,” and **your hands** represents “your actions.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [have promised it and you have fulfilled it by your actions]
See how you translated this name in 7:18.
See how you translated the similar expression in 22:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 29:25.

26.note: Following the custom of his culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred, his own **great name**. Alternate translation: [I have solemnly promised, guaranteeing it by my great name]

26.q: אִם יִהְיֶה֩ ע֨וֹד שְׁמִ֜⁠י נִקְרָ֣א בְּ⁠פִ֣י כָּל אִ֣ישׁ יְהוּדָ֗ה
26.note: The expression **My name will no longer be called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No man of Judah will any longer call my name with his mouth]
Here, **the mouth** represents “the speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [aloud by any man of Judah]

Following the custom of their culture, the people of Judah would swear an oath and guarantee it by something that they held sacred, **the life of Lord Yahweh**. Alternate translation: [I swear this to be true, just as surely as Lord Yahweh is alive]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4.
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:3.
See how you translated the similar expression in 42:17.

27.note: Yahweh is using **watching over them for harm and not for good** as a common expression of the culture to mean “paying close attention to them in order to harm them and not to do good to them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [paying close attention to them so that I can harm them and not do good to them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 42:17.

28.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **fugitives** who have escaped from **the sword**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the people who escape being killed in battle]

Yahweh is using **men of number** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a few men,” that is, so few that they could easily be counted. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [only a very few men]

Yahweh is speaking as if a **word** were a person who could **stand**. It means that what someone says proves to be true. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whose word will prove to be true, from me or from them]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [whether the word from me or the word from them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 42:22.

29.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8.

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **stand** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [my words will surely stand]

30.note: The word **Hophra** is the name of a man. He was the king of Egypt at this time, and **Pharaoh** was the title of the kings of Egypt.

Here, **the hand** represents “the power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the power of his enemies and into the power of the ones seeking his life]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:7.
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:7.
See how you translated the similar expression in 39:16.
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:3.
